When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: Machine Learning Topological Invariants with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn topological invariants from local inputs and generalize to predict winding numbers for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that neural networks can successfully learn global topological invariants from local Hamiltonian inputs, generalize to predict winding numbers beyond the training range, and internally learn the discrete winding number formula.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn global and nonlinear topological features from local inputs and exhibit strong generalization power, opening possibilities for using machine learning to study topological physics.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can predict topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not included in the training data.
Convolutional networks outperform fully-connected networks due to their inherent translation symmetry, which matches the symmetry of the winding number problem.
By analyzing the internal function of the convolutional network, the authors confirm it learns the discrete version of the winding number formula.
Regularization techniques like L2 regularization can harm generalization when training data are noise-free, but become beneficial when noise is present.
If training data are restricted to a specific model (e.g., the SSH model), the network may learn shortcuts based on local symmetries and fail to generalize to more general Hamiltonians.
papers.limitation:
Regularization techniques can be detrimental to generalization when the training data are noise-free.
If the training data are restricted to a specific model with additional symmetries, the neural network may learn shortcuts and fail to generalize to more general cases.
future_direction: Generalize the results to topological models in higher dimensions and other symmetry classes.
Apply the trained network to analyze data from quantum simulators.
papers.abstract: In this Letter we supervisedly train neural networks to distinguish different topological phases in the context of topological band insulators. After training with Hamiltonians of one-dimensional insulators with chiral symmetry, the neural network can predict their topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers that are not included in the training data. These results show a remarkable success that the neural network can capture the global and nonlinear topological features of quantum phases from local inputs. By opening up the neural network, we confirm that the network does learn the discrete version of the winding number formula. We also make a couple of remarks regarding the role of the symmetry and the opposite effect of regularization techniques when applying machine learning to physical systems.

papers.title: Rapid Identification of X-ray Diffraction Spectra Based on Very Limited Data by Interpretable Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a convolutional neural network be trained with limited experimental data to achieve rapid one-to-one identification of X-ray diffraction spectra?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a CNN model trained on noise-augmented theoretical XRD spectra for rapid one-to-one identification of individual materials, achieving 96.7% Top-5 accuracy and providing interpretability through class activation maps.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model enables accurate one-by-one identification of XRD spectra using noise-augmented data and provides interpretability through CAMs, with potential applications in various characterization techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieves 96.7% Top-5 accuracy for identifying 1012 MOFs from XRD spectra.
Noise-based data augmentation from experimental spectra enables effective training with limited data.
Neighborhood components analysis shows that XRD spectra from the same material cluster together.
Class activation maps reveal that the CNN focuses on main peaks for identification, similar to expert analysis.
The model is robust to peak shifts, intensity variations, and noise when combined with filtering techniques.
papers.limitation: Lower crystallinity and high noise in experimental spectra can reduce classification accuracy.
future_direction: Expanding the method to other characterization techniques such as Raman, NMR, and FTIR.
papers.abstract: Large volumes of data from material characterizations call for rapid and automatic data analysis to accelerate materials discovery. Herein, we report a convolutional neural network (CNN) that was trained based on theoretic data and very limited experimental data for fast identification of experimental X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). To augment the data for training the model, noise was extracted from experimental spectra and shuffled, then merged with the main peaks that were extracted from theoretical spectra to synthesize new spectra. For the first time, one-to-one material identification was achieved. The optimized model showed the highest identification accuracy of 96.7% for the Top 5 ranking among a dataset of 1012 MOFs. Neighborhood components analysis (NCA) on the experimental XRD spectra shows that the spectra from the same material are clustered in groups in the NCA map. Analysis on the class activation maps of the last CNN layer further discloses the mechanism by which the CNN model successfully identifies individual MOFs from the XRD spectra. This CNN model trained by the data-augmentation technique would not only open numerous potential applications for identifying XRD spectra for different materials, but also pave avenues to autonomously analyze data by other characterization tools such as FTIR, Raman, and NMR.

papers.title: Explaining the Machine Learning Solution of the Ising Model
papers.research_question: How can we explain the results from machine learning models applied to the Ising model? Specifically, how do PCA and a simple neural network identify phases and the critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that PCA identifies the order parameter and temperature as the control variable, and that a single-layer neural network informed by symmetry can accurately predict the critical temperature, with the explanation revealing that the network learns to use the magnetization direction.
papers.conclusion: The explanation of the strategies used by simpler ML models indicates the directions that can be taken to fully explain more sophisticated ones, opening the ML black-boxes and paving the way to extract physical laws from model parameters.
papers.key_findings:
PCA not only identifies the magnetization as the order parameter but also shows that the greatest variance is in the direction of the temperature gradient.
A single-layer neural network (SLNN) with no hidden layers, informed by spin inversion symmetry, can accurately estimate the critical temperature of the Ising model.
The SLNN works by aligning its weight vector with the magnetization direction and scaling the argument to separate phases.
A one-hidden-layer NN with two units can solve the general case without sign restriction, and the output layer combines the hidden units' outputs to correct labeling.
The explanation allows predicting the minimal NN architecture needed for more complex phase transitions.
papers.limitation:
The method may require more hidden units or non-linear techniques for more complex phase diagrams.
It has not yet been possible to extract physical laws from the inferred parameters.
future_direction: Applying the method to other physics systems with more general phase transitions, both classical and quantum.
Extracting physical laws from the parameters of the models.
papers.abstract: As powerful as machine learning (ML) techniques are in solving problems involving data with large dimensionality, explaining the results from the fitted parameters remains a challenging task of utmost importance, especially in physics applications. This work shows how this can be accomplished for the ferromagnetic Ising model, the main target of several ML studies in statistical physics. Here it is demonstrated that the successful unsupervised identification of the phases and order parameter by principal component analysis, a common method in those studies, detects that the magnetization per spin has its greatest variation with the temperature, the actual control parameter of the phase transition. Then, by using a neural network (NN) without hidden layers (the simplest possible) and informed by the symmetry of the Hamiltonian, an explanation is provided for the strategy used in finding the supervised learning solution for the critical temperature of the model's continuous phase transition. This allows the prediction of the minimal extension of the NN to solve the problem when the symmetry is not known, which becomes also explainable. These results pave the way to a physics-informed explainable generalized framework, enabling the extraction of physical laws and principles from the parameters of the models.

papers.title: Beyond performance: How design choices shape chemical language models
papers.research_question: How do design choices (molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, model architecture) influence the performance and chemical interpretability of chemical language models?
papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Decoding Structure-Spectrum Relationships with Physically Organized Latent Spaces
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to construct an interpretable latent space that maps individual structure descriptors to spectral trends in XANES spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RankAAE, a semi-supervised method that constructs an interpretable latent space for spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships by disentangling contributions from multiple structural descriptors.
papers.conclusion: The RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers in interpreting complex scientific data, testing physical hypotheses, and revealing new patterns that extend scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
RankAAE produces a regularized latent space that ensures decoded spectra are physical, unlike standard autoencoders.
The method aligns individual latent dimensions with specific structure descriptors (e.g., oxidation state, coordination number) through a rank constraint.
RankAAE reveals new structure-spectrum relationships that are visually indiscernible in large datasets.
The method works consistently across eight transition metal oxide families (Ti to Cu).
RankAAE enables comparison of different sets of structure descriptors and assesses their importance in capturing spectral variations.
papers.abstract: A new semi-supervised machine learning method for the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships is developed and demonstrated using the specific example of interpreting X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra. This method constructs a one-to-one mapping between individual structure descriptors and spectral trends. Specifically, an adversarial autoencoder is augmented with a novel rank constraint (RankAAE). The RankAAE methodology produces a continuous and interpretable latent space, where each dimension can track an individual structure descriptor. As a part of this process, the model provides a robust and quantitative measure of the structure-spectrum relationship by decoupling intertwined spectral contributions from multiple structural characteristics. This makes it ideal for spectral interpretation and the discovery of new descriptors. The capability of this procedure is showcased by considering five local structure descriptors and a database of over fifty thousand simulated XANES spectra across eight first-row transition metal oxide families. The resulting structure-spectrum relationships not only reproduce known trends in the literature, but also reveal unintuitive ones that are visually indiscernible in large data sets. The results suggest that the RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers to interpret complex scientific data, test physical hypotheses, and reveal new patterns that extend scientific insight.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box: Learning the relevance of many-body functions in Neural Network potentials
papers.research_question: How can machine learned coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks be interpreted in terms of physically meaningful many-body contributions to the total energy?
papers.core_contribution: Extends GNN-LRP to interpret coarse-grained neural network potentials, showing the learned energy can be decomposed into physically meaningful many-body contributions.
papers.conclusion: GNN-LRP provides a way to interpret machine learned coarse-grained potentials, showing the learned interactions are physically meaningful and offering insights into molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
For methane and water, 2-body relevance scores show repulsive interactions at short distances and, for water, stabilizing interactions at the first solvation shell.
3-body interactions are crucial for water to recover structural properties, with relevance scores indicating stabilizing and destabilizing contributions.
For protein NTL9, relevance scores identify stabilizing interactions in the folded state and can distinguish between two folding pathways.
The method can analyze the effect of mutations by changing bead embeddings, showing the model learns amino-acid specific interactions.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) learn similar underlying physical interactions despite different functional representations.
future_direction: Refining the concepts to provide greater insight and systematic choice of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One of the main criticisms to machine learned potentials is that the energy inferred by the network is not as interpretable as in more traditional approaches where a simpler functional form is used. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks (GNN). We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. On these examples, we show that the neural network potentials can be in practice decomposed in relevance contributions to different orders, that can be directly interpreted and provide physical insights on the systems of interest.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Neural Networks as Physics-Consistent Surrogates: An \textit{Explainable AI} Validation Framework for Learning Constitutive Relations
papers.research_question: How can neural networks for constitutive modeling of solid materials be validated and interpreted to confirm they learn physically meaningful principles rather than merely curve-fitting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops and applies a Physics-Explainable AI (XAI) framework to validate that neural network surrogates for constitutive modeling learn underlying physical mechanisms (stiffness, history-dependence, temporal damping) rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.conclusion: The Physics-XAI framework successfully validates that neural constitutive models learn physically interpretable representations of stiffness, path dependence, and fractional-order memory, transforming them from black boxes into transparent, mechanically grounded glass boxes.
papers.key_findings:
For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (Grad Input and Integrated Gradients) match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness.
For elastoplasticity, SHAP and PCA show the RNN internalizes path-dependent memory, with plastic strain identified as the dominant feature governing stress prediction.
For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of GRU layers reveal a temporal hierarchy encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory.
The Physics-Aware Distillation (PAD) procedure extracts interpretable material constants (e.g., Mooney-Rivlin coefficients) from the trained neural networks.
Quantitative metrics (MSE, MAE, R2, attribution correlations) confirm high fidelity and physical consistency across all three material models.
papers.limitation: The work focuses on uniaxial settings and noise-free synthetic data.
future_direction: Extend to multiaxial loading, anisotropic materials, and experimental datasets.
Integrate XAI with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).
Incorporate uncertainty quantification and robustness analysis for verification and validation.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a Physics-\textit{Explainable AI} (XAI) framework to validate and interpret neural networks for the constitutive modeling of solid materials. The study bridges the gap between data-driven models and continuum mechanics by applying a suite of explainability methods to neural networks trained on three distinct material behaviors: hyperelasticity (\textit{Mooney-Rivlin}), elastoplasticity (\textit{Chaboche}), and viscoelasticity (\textit{Fractional Zener}). First, high-fidelity surrogate models, including dense feed-forward networks, LSTMs, and GRUs, are trained on synthetically generated data to accurately capture complex material responses. The core of the work then employs XAI techniques to "open the black box" and confirm that the networks learn physically meaningful principles. For hyperelasticity, gradient-based attributions (\textit{Grad Input} (GI)) successfully match the analytical tangent modulus, proving the network learned material stiffness. For elastoplasticity, \textit{SHapley Additive exPlanations} (SHAP) and \textit{Principal Component Analysis} (PCA) demonstrate the \textit{Recurrent Neural Network} (RNN) internalizes path-dependent memory, with SHAP identifying \textit{plastic strain} as the dominant feature governing the stress prediction. For viscoelasticity, latent-space and wavelet analyses of the \textit{Gated Recurrent Unit. } GRU layers reveal a clear temporal hierarchy, with different layers encoding instantaneous elastic response, intermediate relaxation, and long-term fractional memory. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the XAI framework can verify that the neural networks are not merely curve-fitting but are, in fact, learning the underlying physical mechanisms of stiffness, history-dependence, and temporal damping.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Analyzing Atomic Interactions in Molecules as Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do machine learning force fields (MLFFs) such as SchNet and PaiNN learn underlying physicochemical concepts from data, and how well do their predictions align with known chemical principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops an explainable AI (XAI) framework based on GNN-LRP to analyze atomic interactions in machine learning force fields, and finds that models deviating from fundamental chemical principles produce unstable molecular dynamics trajectories despite high prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed XAI framework provides a way to understand and improve machine learning force fields by assessing their adherence to chemical principles, which is crucial for generating stable and physically meaningful simulations.
papers.key_findings:
Interaction strength is atom-type and property dependent.
Intensive properties (e.g., HOMO energy) have a larger interaction range than extensive properties (e.g., atomization energy).
The decay of interaction strength with distance does not follow a polynomial power law as expected from physical principles.
Models exhibit many-body interactions, meaning interaction strength between two atoms depends on the chemical neighborhood.
Models that deviate too far from chemical principles, even with low test errors, produce unstable molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to graph neural networks with a cutoff distance, and the framework's computational complexity is high for large numbers of layers, though approximations mitigate this.
future_direction: Improving ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures and a wider range of molecular properties.
papers.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models have been able to achieve unprecedented accuracies across various prediction tasks in quantum chemistry, it is now apparent that accuracy on a test set alone is not a guarantee for robust chemical modeling such as stable molecular dynamics (MD). To go beyond accuracy, we use explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to develop a general analysis framework for atomic interactions and apply it to the SchNet and PaiNN neural network models. We compare these interactions with a set of fundamental chemical principles to understand how well the models have learned the underlying physicochemical concepts from the data. We focus on the strength of the interactions for different atomic species, how predictions for intensive and extensive quantum molecular properties are made, and analyze the decay and many-body nature of the interactions with interatomic distance. Models that deviate too far from known physical principles produce unstable MD trajectories, even when they have very high energy and force prediction accuracy. We also suggest further improvements to the ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.

papers.title: Detection of Phase Transition via Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks detect phase transitions in physical systems without prior knowledge of the order parameter or critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: A convolutional neural network can detect the phase transition of the 2D Ising model without prior knowledge, and a novel order parameter derived from the network's weight matrix can identify the critical temperature.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks, particularly CNNs, can capture features of phase transitions and can be used to define order parameters that identify critical temperatures in physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrix of the trained CNN shows a domain-like structure with a boundary near the critical temperature.
An order parameter Wsum(β) defined from the weight matrix can be used to extract the critical temperature via fitting.
The extracted critical temperatures for different lattice sizes are consistent with the exact value to within 2-8% accuracy.
The CNN's convolutional filters resemble a real-space renormalization group transformation, capturing local magnetization.
A fully connected neural network also detects the phase transition but with less accuracy than the CNN.
future_direction: Applying the neural network design to other statistical models and non-trivial phases.
papers.abstract:
We design a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) which studies correlation
between discretized inverse temperature and spin configuration of 2D Ising
model and show that it can find a feature of the phase transition without
teaching any a priori information for it. We also define a new order parameter
via the CNN and show that it provides well approximated critical inverse
temperature. In addition, we compare the activation functions for convolution
layer and find that the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is important to detect the
phase transition of 2D Ising model.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: On the flow matching interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we make the intermediate steps of flow matching models interpretable by constraining them to traverse physically meaningful states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to make flow matching interpretable by constraining each flow step to correspond to equilibrium states of a physical process, demonstrated on the 2D Ising model where steps represent thermal transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper addresses the challenge of interpreting diffusion steps in flow-matching models by constraining trajectories to physically meaningful transitions, demonstrating preserved physical fidelity with computational speedups over Monte Carlo methods and correct capture of phase transitions and critical phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed for larger lattices.
Each vector field update represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space.
The learned decoder generates configurations that closely resemble true physical behavior, especially near the critical temperature.
The method correctly captures phase transitions and critical phenomena.
The approach transforms abstract flow evolution into concrete, physically-grounded dynamics.
future_direction: Applying the framework to different diffusion models and other physical systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models based on flow matching have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet they suffer from a fundamental limitation: the lack of interpretability in their intermediate generation steps. In fact these models learn to transform noise into data through a series of vector field updates, however the meaning of each step remains opaque. We address this problem by proposing a general framework constraining each flow step to be sampled from a known physical distribution. Flow trajectories are mapped to (and constrained to traverse) the equilibrium states of the simulated physical process. We implement this approach through the 2D Ising model in such a way that flow steps become thermal equilibrium points along a parametric cooling schedule. Our proposed architecture includes an encoder that maps discrete Ising configurations into a continuous latent space, a flow-matching network that performs temperature-driven diffusion, and a projector that returns to discrete Ising states while preserving physical constraints. We validate this framework across multiple lattice sizes, showing that it preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed as the lattice size increases. In contrast with standard flow matching, each vector field represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space. This demonstrates that embedding physical semantics into generative flows transforms opaque neural trajectories into interpretable physical processes.

papers.title: Representation Learning on a Random Lattice
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a geometric model of data distributions as random lattices, analyzed via percolation theory, and categorizes learned features into context, component, and surface features.
papers.conclusion: The random lattice model provides a geometric perspective on data distributions that is qualitatively consistent with recent mechanistic interpretability findings and suggests directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be categorized into context, component, and surface features based on data distribution geometry.
A power-law distribution of useful latent features emerges from the random lattice model.
Sparse dictionary learning methods like SAEs are most useful in subcritical regimes where feature sparsity predominates.
Component features may require multidimensional representations, contrary to the linear representation hypothesis.
The model suggests that SAEs may imperfectly recover true features that have a nested hierarchy, consistent with feature splitting observations.
future_direction: Explore interpretability methods sensitive to finding multidimensional features.
Develop SAE variants with inductive biases for hierarchical structure, such as nested groups of latents.
Develop a richer model with weighted bonds between dataset elements to better capture inexact family resemblances.
papers.abstract: Decomposing a deep neural network's learned representations into interpretable features could greatly enhance its safety and reliability. To better understand features, we adopt a geometric perspective, viewing them as a learned coordinate system for mapping an embedded data distribution. We motivate a model of a generic data distribution as a random lattice and analyze its properties using percolation theory. Learned features are categorized into context, component, and surface features. The model is qualitatively consistent with recent findings in mechanistic interpretability and suggests directions for future research.

papers.title: Restyling Unsupervised Concept Based Interpretable Networks with Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the visualization and interpretation of learnt unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks for large-scale images?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VisCoIN, a novel architecture for unsupervised concept-based interpretable networks that maps concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model, enabling high-quality visualization and interactive interpretation of learnt concepts.
papers.conclusion: VisCoIN effectively leverages pretrained generative models to improve visualization and interpretation of unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks, achieving high prediction performance and learning more faithful and consistent concepts.
papers.key_findings:
VisCoIN achieves comparable prediction accuracy to baseline methods while improving reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity.
The learnt concepts in VisCoIN are more faithful and consistent compared to previous unsupervised CoINs.
The visualization pipeline based on the generative model allows for granular and interactive interpretation of concepts by modifying concept activations and observing changes in generated images.
papers.limitation:
Cannot guarantee that concepts precisely correspond to human concepts and may encode additional information.
System quality is limited by the quality of the pretrained generative model.
Linear trajectories in latent space may not be optimal for latent traversals.
papers.abstract: Developing inherently interpretable models for prediction has gained prominence in recent years. A subclass of these models, wherein the interpretable network relies on learning high-level concepts, are valued because of closeness of concept representations to human communication. However, the visualization and understanding of the learnt unsupervised dictionary of concepts encounters major limitations, especially for large-scale images. We propose here a novel method that relies on mapping the concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The use of a generative model enables high quality visualization, and lays out an intuitive and interactive procedure for better interpretation of the learnt concepts by imputing concept activations and visualizing generated modifications. Furthermore, leveraging pretrained generative models has the additional advantage of making the training of the system more efficient. We quantitatively ascertain the efficacy of our method in terms of accuracy of the interpretable prediction network, fidelity of reconstruction, as well as faithfulness and consistency of learnt concepts. The experiments are conducted on multiple image recognition benchmarks for large-scale images. Project page available at https://jayneelparekh.github.io/VisCoIN_project_page/

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Language Models For protein design
papers.research_question: How can we design a protein language model that is controllable, interpretable, and debuggable without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Language Models, a novel architecture that incorporates human-understandable concepts via a concept bottleneck layer, enabling precise control, interpretability, and debugging while maintaining performance comparable to traditional language models.
papers.conclusion: CB-pLM provides a framework for controllable, interpretable, and debuggable language models without sacrificing performance, making it particularly valuable for high-stakes domains like protein design.
papers.key_findings:
CB-pLM achieves 3x better control in terms of change in concept magnitude and 16% improvement in control accuracy compared to baselines.
CB-pLM maintains pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models.
CB-pLM enables multi-concept interventions with high accuracy (94% control accuracy).
CB-pLM allows interpretability and debugging by inspecting the linear decoder weights, revealing concept-token relationships.
CB-pLM can generalize to unseen concept combinations, as demonstrated on ColorMNIST.
future_direction: Extending CB-LM to other domains and architectures
Adding new concepts to a trained CB-LM via fine-tuning
Generalization to new concept combinations
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Protein Language Models (CB-pLM), a generative masked language model with a layer where each neuron corresponds to an interpretable concept. Our architecture offers three key benefits: i) Control: We can intervene on concept values to precisely control the properties of generated proteins, achieving a 3 times larger change in desired concept values compared to baselines. ii) Interpretability: A linear mapping between concept values and predicted tokens allows transparent analysis of the model's decision-making process. iii) Debugging: This transparency facilitates easy debugging of trained models. Our models achieve pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models, demonstrating that interpretability does not compromise performance. While adaptable to any language model, we focus on masked protein language models due to their importance in drug discovery and the ability to validate our model's capabilities through real-world experiments and expert knowledge. We scale our CB-pLM from 24 million to 3 billion parameters, making them the largest Concept Bottleneck Models trained and the first capable of generative language modeling.

papers.title: Variational Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: How can we achieve unsupervised discovery of interpretable features and controllable generation in high-dimensional data using sparse coding within variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Variational Sparse Coding (VSC) model, a variational autoencoder with a spike and slab prior, which achieves superior unsupervised feature disentanglement and enables controllable generation when the number of true sources of variation is unknown and attributes appear in different combinations.
papers.conclusion: The VSC model retrieves non-linear sparse representations of data, capable of disentangling sources of variation where attributes can be present or absent in different combinations and the total number of factors is unknown a priori.
papers.key_findings:
VSC outperforms standard β-VAE and β-TCVAE in feature disentanglement on data where the number of true sources is unknown and objects display different combinations of attributes.
VSC recovers sparse latent representations that capture both discrete and continuous sources of variation in data.
The model enables unsupervised conditional generation, feature interpolation, and investigation of feature relationships between objects.
A closed-form expression for the KL divergence between spike and slab distributions and a spike variable warm-up training strategy are key contributions for efficient model training.
VSC maintains strong disentanglement properties even when the latent dimensionality is much larger than the number of true generating features.
papers.limitation: The model suffers from posterior collapse during training, where some latent variables become inactive.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised discovery of interpretable features and controllable generation with highdimensional data are currently major challenges in machine learning, with applications in data visualisation, clustering and artificial data synthesis. We propose a model based on variational auto-encoders (VAEs) in which interpretation is induced through latent space sparsity with a mixture of Spike and Slab distributions as prior. We derive an evidence lower bound for this model and propose a specific training method for recovering disentangled features as sparse elements in latent vectors. In our experiments, we demonstrate superior disentanglement performance to standard VAE approaches when an estimate of the number of true sources of variation is not available and objects display different combinations of attributes. Furthermore, the new model provides unique capabilities, such as recovering feature exploitation, synthesising samples that share attributes with a given input object and controlling both discrete and continuous features upon generation.

papers.title: How does My Model Fail? Automatic Identification and Interpretation of Physical Plausibility Failure Modes with Matryoshka Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we automatically identify and interpret specific physical plausibility error patterns in generative models to enable targeted model improvements?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce Matryoshka Transcoders, a framework for automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features in generative models via hierarchical sparse feature learning on classifier representations, enabling interpretable benchmarking and failure mode analysis.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka Transcoders enable automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features, providing a hierarchical sparse feature learning approach that reveals systematic failure modes across generative models and paves the way for targeted improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka Transcoders outperform baseline methods (SAE, Matryoshka SAE, Transcoder) in both population-based and description-based feature relevance metrics.
The method discovers diverse physical plausibility failure modes (e.g., anatomical distortions, malformed text, implausible styles) and attaches accurate natural language descriptions.
Benchmarking eight generative models reveals FLUX achieves the best physical plausibility (lowest mean error count) while SDXL-turbo exhibits the most violations.
A feature relevance bottleneck phenomenon is observed where features cluster at two extremes (70-80% and >95% relevance), justifying focus on highly selective features.
Smaller dictionary sizes yield more focused and relevant features, while larger sizes provide broader coverage, motivating the use of nested dictionaries.
papers.limitation:
Discovered features are not yet incorporated into training pipelines to actively reduce physical plausibility failures.
Certain subtle or rare physical violations may be underrepresented if training data lacks sufficient examples, creating potential evaluation blind spots.
The feature absorption phenomenon is not quantified for visual inputs due to the high-dimensional, continuous nature of image representations.
The framework focuses only on physical plausibility, leaving other quality dimensions (aesthetics, semantic faithfulness, social biases) for future work.
future_direction: Incorporating discovered features into training pipelines to actively reduce physical plausibility failures.
Developing methods to measure feature absorption rate in vision models.
Extending the framework to other quality dimensions such as aesthetics, semantic faithfulness, and social biases.
papers.abstract: Although recent generative models are remarkably capable of producing instruction-following and realistic outputs, they remain prone to notable physical plausibility failures. Though critical in applications, these physical plausibility errors often escape detection by existing evaluation methods. Furthermore, no framework exists for automatically identifying and interpreting specific physical error patterns in natural language, preventing targeted model improvements. We introduce Matryoshka Transcoders, a novel framework for the automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features in generative models. Our approach extends the Matryoshka representation learning paradigm to transcoder architectures, enabling hierarchical sparse feature learning at multiple granularity levels. By training on intermediate representations from a physical plausibility classifier and leveraging large multimodal models for interpretation, our method identifies diverse physics-related failure modes without manual feature engineering, achieving superior feature relevance and feature accuracy compared to existing approaches. We utilize the discovered visual patterns to establish a benchmark for evaluating physical plausibility in generative models. Our analysis of eight state-of-the-art generative models provides valuable insights into how these models fail to follow physical constraints, paving the way for further model improvements.

papers.title: On the Ability of Deep Networks to Learn Symmetries from Data: A Neural Kernel Theory
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do deep networks generalize symmetry invariance to partially observed classes when trained on data with partially observed symmetries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a neural kernel theory showing that deep networks cannot learn symmetries not embedded in their architecture, and generalization on symmetric datasets requires the local data structure to dominate the non-local symmetric structure in kernel space.
papers.conclusion: Conventional deep networks are unable to learn symmetries not embedded in their architecture, and successful generalization on symmetric datasets occurs only when the local data structure prevails over the non-local symmetric structure in kernel space.
papers.key_findings:
Generalization error on symmetric datasets is characterized by a spectral error formula depending on kernel eigenvalues.
Deep networks (MLP, CNN, ViT) fail to extrapolate symmetries from partially observed data unless the number of sampled transformations is large.
The neural kernel theory accurately predicts the generalization behavior of finite-width networks on rotated-MNIST.
Equivariant architectures (e.g., CNNs) succeed when the architecture matches the data symmetry.
Conventional deep networks lack a mechanism to learn symmetries that have not been explicitly embedded in their architecture a priori.
papers.limitation:
The theory is developed for finite groups (cyclic and non-abelian) but not for continuous groups.
The study focuses on symmetries native to the dataset space, not latent space symmetries.
future_direction: Extend the theory to continuous groups such as SO(3).
Study symmetries in latent space affecting the dataset indirectly.
Use the theory to guide the design of architectures and training procedures able to learn symmetries from data.
papers.abstract: Symmetries (transformations by group actions) are present in many datasets, and leveraging them holds considerable promise for improving predictions in machine learning. In this work, we aim to understand when and how deep networks -- with standard architectures trained in a standard, supervised way -- learn symmetries from data. Inspired by real-world scenarios, we study a classification paradigm where data symmetries are only partially observed during training: some classes include all transformations of a cyclic group, while others -- only a subset. In the infinite-width limit, where kernel analogies apply, we derive a neural kernel theory of symmetry learning. The group-cyclic nature of the dataset allows us to analyze the Gram matrix of neural kernels in the Fourier domain; here we find a simple characterization of the generalization error as a function of class separation (signal) and class-orbit density (noise). This characterization reveals that generalization can only be successful when the local structure of the data prevails over its non-local, symmetry-induced structure, in the kernel space defined by the architecture. We extend our theoretical treatment to any finite group, including non-abelian groups. Our framework also applies to equivariant architectures (e.g., CNNs), and recovers their success in the special case where the architecture matches the inherent symmetry of the data. Empirically, our theory reproduces the generalization failure of finite-width networks (MLP, CNN, ViT) trained on partially observed versions of rotated-MNIST. We conclude that conventional deep networks lack a mechanism to learn symmetries that have not been explicitly embedded in their architecture a priori. Our framework could be extended to guide the design of architectures and training procedures able to learn symmetries from data.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
