Here, we develop an unsupervised style-based image generation model to identify perceptually relevant dimensions for translucent material appearances from photographs. We find our model, with its layer-wise latent representation, can synthesize images of diverse and realistic materials. Importantly, without supervision, human-understandable scene attributes, including the object's shape, material, and body color, spontaneously emerge in the model's layer-wise latent space in a scale-specific manner. By embedding an image into the learned latent space, we can manipulate specific layers' latent code to modify the appearance of the object in the image. Specifically, we find that manipulation on the early-layers (coarse spatial scale) transforms the object's shape, while manipulation on the later-layers (fine spatial scale) modifies its body color. The middle-layers of the latent space selectively encode translucency features and manipulation of such layers coherently modifies the translucency appearance, without changing the object's shape or body color. Moreover, we find the middle-layers of the latent space can successfully predict human translucency ratings, suggesting that translucent impressions are established in mid-to-low spatial scale features. This layer-wise latent representation allows us to systematically discover perceptually relevant image features for human translucency perception. Together, our findings reveal that learning the scale-specific statistical structure of natural images might be crucial for humans to efficiently represent material properties across contexts.

papers.title: Measuring Orthogonality in Representations of Generative Models
papers.research_question: Is the orthogonality of generative factor subspaces in learned representations a better indicator of their quality for downstream tasks than traditional disentanglement metrics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two new metrics, Importance-Weighted Orthogonality (IWO) and Importance-Weighted Rank (IWR), and a method called Generative Component Analysis (GCA) to compute them, showing that orthogonality of generative factor subspaces correlates more strongly with downstream task performance than traditional disentanglement metrics.
papers.conclusion: The utility of a representation is more closely related to its orthogonality than its disentanglement, offering a new direction for evaluating and improving unsupervised learning models.
papers.key_findings:
IWO and IWR consistently show stronger correlations with downstream task performance (e.g., classification, regression, segmentation) than traditional disentanglement metrics like MIG and DCI.
Representation quality is more closely related to the orthogonality of independent generative processes than to their disentanglement (alignment with the canonical basis).
Generative Component Analysis (GCA) effectively identifies the latent subspaces corresponding to generative factors and their importance weights.
Orthogonal but entangled representations can be as effective as disentangled ones for downstream tasks.
The proposed metrics are resilient to changes in dataset size and non-linear encoding functions.
papers.limitation: GCA requires supervision from the generative factors, information that may not always be available.
papers.abstract: In unsupervised representation learning, models aim to distill essential features from high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional learned representations, guided by inductive biases. Understanding the characteristics that make a good representation remains a topic of ongoing research. Disentanglement of independent generative processes has long been credited with producing high-quality representations. However, focusing solely on representations that adhere to the stringent requirements of most disentanglement metrics, may result in overlooking many high-quality representations, well suited for various downstream tasks. These metrics often demand that generative factors be encoded in distinct, single dimensions aligned with the canonical basis of the representation space. Motivated by these observations, we propose two novel metrics: Importance-Weighted Orthogonality (IWO) and Importance-Weighted Rank (IWR). These metrics evaluate the mutual orthogonality and rank of generative factor subspaces. Throughout extensive experiments on common downstream tasks, over several benchmark datasets and models, IWO and IWR consistently show stronger correlations with downstream task performance than traditional disentanglement metrics. Our findings suggest that representation quality is closer related to the orthogonality of independent generative processes rather than their disentanglement, offering a new direction for evaluating and improving unsupervised learning models.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
papers.research_question: Why do neural networks arrive at particular computational strategies when trained on algebraic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that margin maximization can fully specify the features learned by neural networks on algebraic tasks, explaining why networks arrive at particular computational strategies such as Fourier features for modular addition.
papers.conclusion: Margin maximization fully specifies the features learned on algebraic tasks, providing insight into why networks adopt particular computational strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum margin solutions for modular addition use neurons that are sparse in Fourier space, each neuron corresponding to a single frequency.
For sparse parity, maximum margin solutions have neurons that assign equal magnitude weights to relevant bits and satisfy a sign condition.
For finite group operations, maximum margin solutions use neurons that correspond to irreducible representations of the group.
Neural networks trained with gradient descent and small regularization approach the maximum margin solution, and their learned features match the theoretical predictions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple architectures (one-hidden layer networks) and synthetic algebraic tasks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigate margin maximization in more realistic settings.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations learned by neural networks is a cornerstone challenge in the science of machine learning. While there have been significant recent strides in some cases towards understanding how neural networks implement specific target functions, this paper explores a complementary question -- why do networks arrive at particular computational strategies? Our inquiry focuses on the algebraic learning tasks of modular addition, sparse parities, and finite group operations. Our primary theoretical findings analytically characterize the features learned by stylized neural networks for these algebraic tasks. Notably, our main technique demonstrates how the principle of margin maximization alone can be used to fully specify the features learned by the network. Specifically, we prove that the trained networks utilize Fourier features to perform modular addition and employ features corresponding to irreducible group-theoretic representations to perform compositions in general groups, aligning closely with the empirical observations of Nanda et al. and Chughtai et al. More generally, we hope our techniques can help to foster a deeper understanding of why neural networks adopt specific computational strategies.

papers.title: Atomic-level interpretable multimodal graph neural network for predicting carbon dioxide adsorption in metal-organic frameworks
papers.research_question: How can we predict CO₂ adsorption in metal-organic frameworks using an interpretable multimodal graph neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MMAGNN, a multimodal graph neural network that integrates graph and 3D point cloud data to predict CO₂ adsorption in MOFs with atomic-level interpretability via attention weights.
papers.conclusion: MMAGNN utilizes spatial features and atomic interactions to accurately predict CO₂ adsorption and identify adsorption sites, enhancing prediction accuracy and aiding in MOF design for carbon capture.
papers.key_findings:
MMAGNN achieves higher prediction accuracy than CGCNN and ALIGNN across various pressures, with improvements in MAE, RMSE, and R².
The multimodal design reduces redundant information and feature interference, improving prediction accuracy and stability.
The attention-based interpreter identifies atoms with high attention scores that coincide with CO₂ adsorption sites, validating model interpretability.
MMAGNN effectively captures both local atomic interactions and global pore structure features.
The model generalizes well to modified MOFs like UiO-66-NH₂, correctly shifting attention to new adsorption sites.
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous crystalline materials with strong potential for CO₂ capture because their structures and chemistries are highly tunable. However, their vast compositional and structural search space hampers efficient prediction of adsorption performance. Here we introduce MMAGNN, a multimodal MOF adsorption graph neural network that integrates graph representations and three-dimensional atomic coordinates. MMAGNN employs graph neural networks (GNNs) with attention mechanisms to extract and fuse molecular and spatial features, and incorporates a Transformer-based interpreter to quantify the contribution of individual atoms to adsorption. We find that the multimodal design reduces redundant information and feature interference, improving prediction accuracy and stability. Validation against adsorption density distributions confirms that MMAGNN learns interatomic interactions and pore-structure information and accurately predicts CO₂ adsorption sites. This interpretable framework provides high-throughput screening and rational design of high-performance MOFs for carbon-capture applications. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous crystalline materials with tunable chemistry and pores, making them promising for CO₂ capture. This work introduces the Multimodal MOF Adsorption Graph Neural Network, fusing atomic graphs and 3D point clouds to predict CO₂ adsorption and produce atom-level attention maps highlighting adsorption sites.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Black Boxes and Looking Glasses: Multilevel Symmetries, Reflection Planes, and Convex Optimization in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: Is there a fundamental difference in the nature of functions learned by deep networks, as opposed to shallow networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that training deep narrow networks with absolute value activation is equivalent to convex Lasso problems, revealing that deep networks learn multilevel symmetries via reflections of training data.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves an equivalence between neural networks and Lasso problems with novel geometric features, and suggests that multi-level symmetries may hold for standard ReLU networks as future work.
papers.key_findings:
Training deep neural networks with absolute value activation can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems.
Deep networks favor symmetric structures, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries (symmetries within symmetries).
The Lasso features represent distances to reflection hyperplanes that are spanned by training data and orthogonal to optimal weight vectors.
For 3-layer networks, explicit Lasso dictionaries are given and the optimal first-layer weight is orthogonal to a subset of augmented training data.
Neural networks trained using LLM embeddings learn reflection features similar to those predicted by the Lasso model.
papers.limitation: The choice of absolute value activation and ℓ1 regularization is needed for analytic tractability, which may limit direct applicability to standard ReLU networks.
future_direction: Extensions to ReLU networks.
Analysis of Lasso solution sets and stationary points for higher dimensional data.
Investigation of reflection features in wider ReLU architectures with higher-dimensional data.
papers.abstract: We show that training deep neural networks (DNNs) with absolute value activation and arbitrary input dimension can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems with novel features expressed using geometric algebra. This formulation reveals geometric structures encoding symmetry in neural networks. Using the equivalent Lasso form of DNNs, we formally prove a fundamental distinction between deep and shallow networks: deep networks inherently favor symmetric structures in their fitted functions, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries, i.e., symmetries within symmetries. Moreover, Lasso features represent distances to hyperplanes that are reflected across training points. These reflection hyperplanes are spanned by training data and are orthogonal to optimal weight vectors. Numerical experiments support theory and demonstrate theoretically predicted features when training networks using embeddings generated by Large Language Models.

papers.title: Rule Extraction in Trained Feedforward Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can symbolic rules be extracted from trained feedforward deep neural networks to explain their decision-making process, using cosine similarity and first-order logic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the COLOSSUS algorithm, which integrates cosine similarity and first-order logic to extract symbolic rules from trained feedforward deep neural networks, providing explainability by identifying critical neural paths and mapping them to logical formulas.
papers.conclusion: The COLOSSUS algorithm effectively extracts symbolic rules from feedforward deep neural networks using cosine similarity and first-order logic, providing interpretable explanations and identifying critical neural paths, which is valuable for applications requiring transparency.
papers.key_findings:
The COLOSSUS algorithm successfully extracts logical rules from feedforward DNNs by calculating cosine similarity between weight vectors and activation vectors to identify critical neurons.
The method was tested on wine and breast cancer datasets, achieving high explanation accuracy (e.g., 97% for the wine dataset).
The algorithm identifies a critical neural path per class and can regularize the network by extracting smaller subnetworks.
Extracted rules are expressed as well-formed formulas in propositional and first-order logic, directly mappable to dataset features.
A distance function is implemented to resolve class overlaps in the rule validation stage.
papers.limitation:
The method is limited to classical trained feedforward DNNs and does not apply to other architectures like recurrent neural networks or transformers.
The solution has not been tested on datasets with large amounts of features.
future_direction: Extend the method to other neural network architectures such as recurrent neural networks and transformers.
Test the method on datasets with larger numbers of features.
papers.abstract: Explainability is a key aspect of machine learning, necessary for ensuring transparency and trust in decision-making processes. As machine learning models become more complex, the integration of neural and symbolic approaches has emerged as a promising solution to the explainability problem. One effective solution involves using search techniques to extract rules from trained deep neural networks by examining weight and bias values and calculating their correlation with outputs. This article proposes incorporating cosine similarity in this process to narrow down the search space and identify the critical path connecting inputs to final results. Additionally, the integration of first-order logic (FOL) is suggested to provide a more comprehensive and interpretable understanding of the decision-making process. By leveraging cosine similarity and FOL, an innovative algorithm capable of extracting and explaining rule patterns learned by a feedforward trained neural network was developed and tested in two use cases, demonstrating its effectiveness in providing insights into model behavior.

papers.title: Emergence of Quantised Representations Isolated to Anisotropic Functions
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of activation functions (discrete vs. continuous) influence the emergence and organization of discrete representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that activation functions defined by discrete algebraic symmetries (e.g., permutation-equivariance) induce a quantizing inductive bias, leading to discrete, symmetry-organized clusters in representations, whereas functions with continuous symmetries (e.g., orthogonal-equivariance) preserve more continuous representations.
papers.conclusion: The symmetry properties of activation functions act as a strong inductive bias, with discrete symmetries leading to quantized representations and continuous symmetries preserving continuity, implying that many observed interpretability structures are not fundamental but arise from specific architectural choices.
papers.key_findings:
Discrete symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., standard tanh) cause representations to cluster around distinguished directions, leading to quantized, discrete structures.
Continuous symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., isotropic tanh) do not induce such task-agnostic clustering, resulting in more continuous representations.
The observed quantisation effect correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, suggesting potential pathological consequences.
The Privileged-Plane Projective Method (PPP) is introduced as a tool for high-fidelity visualization of representational geometry, preserving both angular and magnitude information.
The findings suggest that many interpretability phenomena (e.g., grandmother neurons, discrete coding) may be contingent on the choice of anisotropic functional forms rather than fundamental to deep learning.
papers.limitation:
The performance analysis (reconstruction error) is preliminary, as the isotropic activation functions are placeholder designs not optimized for performance.
The study is conducted on relatively small autoencoder models; the findings may not generalize directly to larger, more complex architectures like transformers.
future_direction: Further investigation into the pathological implications of function-driven quantisation, such as effects on adversarial robustness and representational capacity.
Exploration of isotropic functional forms in larger model architectures and their potential performance benefits.
Development of a more comprehensive taxonomy of symmetry-defined functional forms and their representational biases.
papers.abstract: Presented is a novel methodology for determining representational structure, which builds upon the existing Spotlight Resonance method. This new tool is used to gain insight into how discrete representations can emerge and organise in autoencoder models, through a controlled ablation study that alters only the activation function. Using this technique, the validity of whether function-driven symmetries can act as implicit inductive biases on representations is determined. Representations are found to tend to discretise when the activation functions are defined through a discrete algebraic permutation-equivariant symmetry. In contrast, they remain continuous under a continuous algebraic orthogonal-equivariant definition. This confirms the hypothesis that the symmetries of network primitives can carry unintended inductive biases, leading to task-independent artefactual structures in representations. The discrete symmetry of contemporary forms is shown to be a strong predictor for the production of symmetry-organised discrete representations emerging from otherwise continuous distributions -- a quantisation effect. This motivates further reassessment of functional forms in common usage due to such unintended consequences. Moreover, this supports a general causal model for a mode in which discrete representations may form, and could constitute a prerequisite for downstream interpretability phenomena, including grandmother neurons, discrete coding schemes, general linear features and a type of Superposition. Hence, this tool and proposed mechanism for the influence of functional form on representations may provide insights into interpretability research. Finally, preliminary results indicate that quantisation of representations correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, reinforcing previous conjectures that this collapse can be detrimental.

papers.title: The Geometry of Concepts: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Structure
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of sparse autoencoder features at atomic, intermediate, and large scales?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features exhibit geometric structure at three scales: atomic crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids), intermediate functional lobes (e.g., for math and code), and large-scale anisotropic point clouds with power-law eigenvalue spectra.
papers.conclusion: SAE features have geometric structure at multiple scales, which may help understand how networks represent features and improve AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Atomic-scale crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids) are revealed after projecting out distractor features using linear discriminant analysis (LDA).
Intermediate-scale functional lobes exist where co-occurring features (e.g., math and code features) cluster together spatially, quantified by mutual information and classification accuracy.
Large-scale point cloud structure is anisotropic with a power-law eigenvalue spectrum, steepest in middle layers.
Clustering entropy (negentropy) is lower in middle layers, indicating more structured representations.
The eigenvalue spectrum of SAE features decays as a power law, more steeply than for raw activations.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain why the observed geometric structure forms.
future_direction: Further work to explain the origin of the geometric structure in SAE features.
Investigate whether variations in structure across layers depend on the prominence of crystals or lobes or have a different origin.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders have recently produced dictionaries of high-dimensional vectors corresponding to the universe of concepts represented by large language models. We find that this concept universe has interesting structure at three levels: 1) The "atomic" small-scale structure contains "crystals" whose faces are parallelograms or trapezoids, generalizing well-known examples such as (man-woman-king-queen). We find that the quality of such parallelograms and associated function vectors improves greatly when projecting out global distractor directions such as word length, which is efficiently done with linear discriminant analysis. 2) The "brain" intermediate-scale structure has significant spatial modularity; for example, math and code features form a "lobe" akin to functional lobes seen in neural fMRI images. We quantify the spatial locality of these lobes with multiple metrics and find that clusters of co-occurring features, at coarse enough scale, also cluster together spatially far more than one would expect if feature geometry were random. 3) The "galaxy" scale large-scale structure of the feature point cloud is not isotropic, but instead has a power law of eigenvalues with steepest slope in middle layers. We also quantify how the clustering entropy depends on the layer.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems. Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Cascade of phase transitions in the training of energy-based models
papers.research_question: How does the Restricted Boltzmann Machine learn features from data, and does it undergo phase transitions during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that RBMs learn features through a cascade of second-order phase transitions, each corresponding to the acquisition of a new principal mode of the data distribution.
papers.conclusion: The learning of RBMs occurs through a cascade of phase transitions, providing insight into the feature encoding process in generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The weights grow exponentially in the direction of the principal components of the dataset.
When the weight norm reaches a critical value, the model undergoes a second-order phase transition, splitting the probability distribution into modes.
These phase transitions are in the mean-field universality class, as confirmed by finite-size scaling.
The learning process involves a cascade of such transitions, progressively refining the learned distribution.
The same phenomena are observed in real datasets like MNIST, CelebA, and HGD.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is primarily for RBMs and simplified models; extending to more complex models like Convolutional EBMs is not straightforward.
The Binary-Gaussian RBM cannot reproduce higher-order correlations in data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other generative models such as Convolutional Energy-Based Models.
Investigating the implications of phase transitions for training strategies and sampling.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the feature encoding process in a prototypical energy-based generative model, the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM). We start with an analytical investigation using simplified architectures and data structures, and end with numerical analysis of real trainings on real datasets. Our study tracks the evolution of the model's weight matrix through its singular value decomposition, revealing a series of phase transitions associated to a progressive learning of the principal modes of the empirical probability distribution. The model first learns the center of mass of the modes and then progressively resolve all modes through a cascade of phase transitions. We first describe this process analytically in a controlled setup that allows us to study analytically the training dynamics. We then validate our theoretical results by training the Bernoulli-Bernoulli RBM on real data sets. By using data sets of increasing dimension, we show that learning indeed leads to sharp phase transitions in the high-dimensional limit. Moreover, we propose and test a mean-field finite-size scaling hypothesis. This shows that the first phase transition is in the same universality class of the one we studied analytically, and which is reminiscent of the mean-field paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic phase transition.

papers.title: Learning Layer-wise Equivariances Automatically using Gradients
papers.research_question: How can the type and amount of layer-wise equivariance symmetries be automatically learned from training data, as opposed to being hard-coded?
papers.core_contribution: A method to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances from data using differentiable Laplace approximations and improved parameterizations of relaxed equivariance, balancing data fit and model complexity.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method allows artificial neural networks to automatically adapt symmetry structure from training data, reducing reliance on trial-and-error in architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
The method can learn convolutional structure in early layers from data, achieving equivalent or improved performance compared to architectures with hard-coded symmetry.
The method can automatically select the most relevant symmetry group from a set of multiple groups, with learned symmetries correlating with data augmentations.
Layers learn to become convolutional, except sometimes at the end of the network where spatial dimensions become 1x1, aligning with common practice.
papers.limitation: The method requires a list of symmetry groups and associated group representations to be considered as candidates.
future_direction: Extending the method to other architecture search problems, such as learning network depth or filter sizes from training data.
papers.abstract: Convolutions encode equivariance symmetries into neural networks leading to better generalisation performance. However, symmetries provide fixed hard constraints on the functions a network can represent, need to be specified in advance, and can not be adapted. Our goal is to allow flexible symmetry constraints that can automatically be learned from data using gradients. Learning symmetry and associated weight connectivity structures from scratch is difficult for two reasons. First, it requires efficient and flexible parameterisations of layer-wise equivariances. Secondly, symmetries act as constraints and are therefore not encouraged by training losses measuring data fit. To overcome these challenges, we improve parameterisations of soft equivariance and learn the amount of equivariance in layers by optimising the marginal likelihood, estimated using differentiable Laplace approximations. The objective balances data fit and model complexity enabling layer-wise symmetry discovery in deep networks. We demonstrate the ability to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances on image classification tasks, achieving equivalent or improved performance over baselines with hard-coded symmetry.

papers.title: Towards a unified and verified understanding of group-operation networks
papers.research_question: How do one-hidden-layer neural networks trained on the binary operation of finite groups compute the group composition, and can a unified and verified explanation be provided?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified mechanistic explanation (the ρ-set circuit) for how neural networks compute group operations, and verifies this explanation by translating it into compact formal proofs that lower-bound model accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The ρ-set circuit explanation unifies previous interpretability results on group-operation networks and is quantitatively validated through compact proofs, representing a step towards rigorous evaluation of mechanistic interpretations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained on group composition implement bi-equivariant ρ-set circuits that approximate the group operation.
The model's learned representation decomposes into irreducible group representations (irreps) acting on discrete ρ-sets.
The explanation can be converted into a compact proof that guarantees a lower bound on model accuracy, providing a quantitative evaluation of interpretability.
Previous explanations (coset concentration and irrep sparsity) are incomplete and do not yield non-vacuous accuracy bounds when formalized.
For a significant fraction of models, the ρ-set explanation yields near-perfect accuracy bounds, while for others, deviations (a-bad, ρ-bad) indicate incomplete understanding.
papers.limitation:
The ρ-set explanation does not hold for all trained models; some exhibit deviations where the projection vector a is not constant (a-bad) or the double sum over the ρ-set is incomplete (ρ-bad).
The analysis and compact proof method are primarily demonstrated on symmetric groups (S5, S4) and the alternating group A5; extension to groups with complex irreps is preliminary.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to groups with complex and quaternionic irreducible representations.
Improve the compact proof bounds, particularly for cross-entropy loss.
Investigate the failure modes (a-bad, ρ-bad) to understand how models compute the group operation in those cases.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work in mechanistic interpretability has focused on reverse-engineering the computation performed by neural networks trained on the binary operation of finite groups. We investigate the internals of one-hidden-layer neural networks trained on this task, revealing previously unidentified structure and producing a more complete description of such models in a step towards unifying the explanations of previous works (Chughtai et al., 2023; Stander et al., 2024). Notably, these models approximate equivariance in each input argument. We verify that our explanation applies to a large fraction of networks trained on this task by translating it into a compact proof of model performance, a quantitative evaluation of the extent to which we faithfully and concisely explain model internals. In the main text, we focus on the symmetric group S5. For models trained on this group, our explanation yields a guarantee of model accuracy that runs 3x faster than brute force and gives a >=95% accuracy bound for 45% of the models we trained. We were unable to obtain nontrivial non-vacuous accuracy bounds using only explanations from previous works.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Model Metamers Reveal Invariances in Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do the invariance properties of graph neural networks (GNNs) compare to human perceptual invariances, and can we quantify and mitigate excessive invariance in GNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a metamer generation technique for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to investigate their representational invariance, revealing excessive invariance in standard architectures and proposing architectural and training modifications to mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for generating model metamers in GNNs to uncover and quantify representational invariance, exposing a misalignment with human perception and providing tools for benchmarking and improving sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Standard GNN architectures exhibit pronounced over-invariance, mapping structurally or semantically different graphs to nearly identical internal activations.
Architectural and training modifications (e.g., replacing ReLU with ELU, adversarial training, adding residual connections) can mitigate over-invariance.
Increasing the hidden layer dimension of a GNN reduces over-invariance by increasing the rank of the model's Jacobian.
Invariance increases with network depth, as feature metamers generated from deeper layers become less similar to the original input.
Cross-model invariance analysis reveals that invariances learned by GNNs comprise both shared components and architecture-specific features.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more graph tasks.
Apply the method to broader model families.
Develop improved metamer generation techniques.
papers.abstract: In recent years, deep neural networks have been extensively employed in perceptual systems to learn representations endowed with invariances, aiming to emulate the invariance mechanisms observed in the human brain. However, studies in the visual and auditory domains have confirmed that significant gaps remain between the invariance properties of artificial neural networks and those of humans. To investigate the invariance behavior within graph neural networks (GNNs), we introduce a model ``metamers'' generation technique. By optimizing input graphs such that their internal node activations match those of a reference graph, we obtain graphs that are equivalent in the model's representation space, yet differ significantly in both structure and node features. Our theoretical analysis focuses on two aspects: the local metamer dimension for a single node and the activation-induced volume change of the metamer manifold. Utilizing this approach, we uncover extreme levels of representational invariance across several classic GNN architectures. Although targeted modifications to model architecture and training strategies can partially mitigate this excessive invariance, they fail to fundamentally bridge the gap to human-like invariance. Finally, we quantify the deviation between metamer graphs and their original counterparts, revealing unique failure modes of current GNNs and providing a complementary benchmark for model evaluation.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: SALSA: Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we learn semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, using SMILES-based autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SALSA, a transformer-autoencoder with a contrastive loss, to learn molecular representations that capture graph-to-graph similarities, resulting in a semantically organized latent space.
papers.conclusion: SALSA learns semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, with improved interpolation and property awareness, and can be applied to other domains with user-defined semantics.
papers.key_findings:
SALSA achieves higher correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance in latent space compared to a naive autoencoder.
SALSA generates more semantically reasonable interpolations between molecules, indicating better semantic continuity.
SALSA implicitly encodes physicochemical properties better than baselines, showing improved property awareness.
The contrastive loss improves structural awareness, while the reconstruction loss acts as a regularizer to prevent degenerative mappings.
SALSA's performance degrades only at very low latent dimensions (e.g., 2 or 4), suggesting robustness down to 8 dimensions.
papers.limitation: The correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance may not hold for molecules that are substantially different
papers.abstract: In deep learning for drug discovery, chemical data are often represented as simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) sequences which allow for straightforward implementation of natural language processing methodologies, one being the sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. However, we observe that training an autoencoder solely on SMILES is insufficient to learn molecular representations that are semantically meaningful, where semantics are defined by the structural (graph-to-graph) similarities between molecules. We demonstrate by example that autoencoders may map structurally similar molecules to distant codes, resulting in an incoherent latent space that does not respect the structural similarities between molecules. To address this shortcoming we propose Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder (SALSA), a transformer-autoencoder modified with a contrastive task, tailored specifically to learn graph-to-graph similarity between molecules. Formally, the contrastive objective is to map structurally similar molecules (separated by a single graph edit) to nearby codes in the latent space. To accomplish this, we generate a novel dataset comprised of sets of structurally similar molecules and opt for a supervised contrastive loss that is able to incorporate full sets of positive samples. We compare SALSA to its ablated counterparts, and show empirically that the composed training objective (reconstruction and contrastive task) leads to a higher quality latent space that is more 1) structurally-aware, 2) semantically continuous, and 3) property-aware.

papers.title: Scale-invariant feature extraction of neural network and renormalization group flow
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and renormalization group (RG) flow, and how does the RBM learn to extract features from spin configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The unsupervised RBM trained on Ising model configurations at various temperatures generates a flow of temperature that approaches the critical point Tc, opposite to the typical RG flow, indicating the RBM learns scale-invariant features.
papers.conclusion: The RBM flow is attracted to the critical point when trained on a wide range of temperatures, and the RBM learns scale-invariant features, showing a connection to RG but with an opposite flow direction.
papers.key_findings:
For type V RBM (trained on configurations from T=0 to T=6), the temperature flow approaches the critical temperature Tc=2.27, making Tc a stable fixed point.
When the hidden layer size Nh is less than or equal to the visible layer size Nv, the flow stabilizes at Tc; for Nh > Nv, the flow eventually moves towards high temperature.
The weight matrix product WW^T reflects spin correlations, and its off-diagonal components decay similarly to spin correlations near Tc.
The eigenvalue spectrum of WW^T for type V RBM shows a gradual decrease without jumps, suggesting scale-invariant feature learning.
The RBM flow is attracted to the features it has learned during training, e.g., type H/L RBMs flow towards high/low temperatures respectively.
future_direction: Investigate the RBM flow for first-order phase transitions, e.g., in the Blume-Capel model.
Study the attractor of RBM flows for human faces to understand value judgments.
Describe the RBM flow as a stochastic process using Langevin or Fokker-Planck equations.
papers.abstract: Theoretical understanding of how a deep neural network (DNN) extracts features from input images is still unclear, but it is widely believed that the extraction is performed hierarchically through a process of coarse graining. It reminds us of the basic renormalization group (RG) concept in statistical physics. In order to explore possible relations between DNN and RG, we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) applied to an Ising model and construct a flow of model parameters (in particular, temperature) generated by the RBM. We show that the unsupervised RBM trained by spin configurations at various temperatures from T=0 to T=6 generates a flow along which the temperature approaches the critical value T_{c}=2.27. This behavior is the opposite of the typical RG flow of the Ising model. By analyzing various properties of the weight matrices of the trained RBM, we discuss why it flows towards T_{c} and how the RBM learns to extract features of spin configurations.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Explainable Representation Learning of Small Quantum States
papers.research_question: Given a set of quantum states that differ solely in their entanglement properties, how will an unsupervised machine learning model learn to represent them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a variational autoencoder (VAE) can learn an interpretable latent representation of quantum states that directly correlates with entanglement measures like concurrence, providing a proof of concept for interpretable machine learning of quantum states.
papers.conclusion: The study establishes the concept of using machine learning techniques to derive interpretable representations for small quantum systems, providing a foundation for extending the methodology to larger quantum systems.
papers.key_findings:
A VAE with one latent dimension can encode the generative parameter α of pure two-qubit states.
When information scrambling is applied, the VAE learns a latent representation that captures entanglement properties rather than local features.
Tuning the regularization strength β leads to a disentangled latent space where a single latent variable encodes the concurrence of the quantum states.
The trained VAE generalizes to random two-qubit states and correctly extracts their concurrence.
The model also generalizes to depolarized two-qubit states and subpartitions of three-qubit states, showing linear correlation with concurrence.
future_direction: Extending the methodology to investigate larger quantum systems.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised machine learning models build an internal representation of their training data without the need for explicit human guidance or feature engineering. This learned representation provides insights into which features of the data are relevant for the task at hand. In the context of quantum physics, training models to describe quantum states without human intervention offers a promising approach to gaining insight into how machines represent complex quantum states. The ability to interpret the learned representation may offer a new perspective on non-trivial features of quantum systems and their efficient representation. We train a generative model on two-qubit density matrices generated by a parameterized quantum circuit. In a series of computational experiments, we investigate the learned representation of the model and its internal understanding of the data. We observe that the model learns an interpretable representation which relates the quantum states to their underlying entanglement characteristics. In particular, our results demonstrate that the latent representation of the model is directly correlated with the entanglement measure concurrence. The insights from this study represent proof of concept towards interpretable machine learning of quantum states. Our approach offers insight into how machines learn to represent small-scale quantum systems autonomously.

papers.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Uncovering Actionable Scientific Insights for Materials Discovery and Design
papers.research_question: How can we extract actionable scientific insights from deep learning models by injecting domain-specific attributes as tunable 'knobs' to understand model behavior and provide guidance for material design?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable deep learning approach that injects domain attributes as tunable knobs in an analysis pipeline, enabling counterfactual understanding and optimization to provide actionable scientific insights for materials discovery.
papers.conclusion: The proposed technique enables the extraction of actionable insights from predictive models by understanding and manipulating domain attributes, which can accelerate materials development processes and is applicable to other scientific domains.
papers.key_findings:
The attribute-guided generative model (attGAN) can generate realistic SEM images with controlled material attributes even with extremely sparse labels.
Forward explanation (sensitivity analysis) reveals how individual material attributes affect the predicted peak stress.
Backward explanation via gradient-based optimization identifies specific attribute changes required to achieve a desired peak stress value.
The method provides actionable insights for material scientists to guide synthesis processes and potentially accelerate material development.
The approach is model-agnostic and can be adapted to understand the behavior of other predictive models.
papers.limitation:
Potential distribution shift from original to reconstructed images, leading to minor prediction shifts.
Built-in variation among predicted values from different image tiles of the same lot due to the regression model's design.
The facetness attribute is not effectively isolated and may be coupled with changes in other attributes like size and polydispersity.
future_direction: Exploring other approaches to build more robust regression models that capture overall qualities from limited data (data-efficient model design).
Addressing the distribution shift between original and reconstructed images.
Improving the isolation of attributes like facetness.
