papers.abstract: The scientific community has been increasingly interested in harnessing the power of deep learning to solve various domain challenges. However, despite the effectiveness in building predictive models, fundamental challenges exist in extracting actionable knowledge from deep neural networks due to their opaque nature. In this work, we propose techniques for exploring the behavior of deep learning models by injecting domain-specific actionable attributes as tunable "knobs" in the analysis pipeline. By incorporating the domain knowledge in a generative modeling framework, we are not only able to better understand the behavior of these black-box models, but also provide scientists with actionable insights that can potentially lead to fundamental discoveries.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: ACES-GNN: can graph neural network learn to explain activity cliffs?
papers.research_question: Can Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) be trained to provide better explanations for activity cliffs (structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences) while also improving prediction accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ACES-GNN framework, which integrates explanation supervision for activity cliffs into GNN training, improving both predictive accuracy and the interpretability of molecular structure-property relationships.
papers.conclusion: ACES-GNN represents a promising direction for improving both the predictivity and interpretability of GNN models in QSAR applications, with the potential to accelerate lead optimization in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ACES-GNN improves explainability (global direction) on 28 out of 30 datasets compared to unsupervised GNNs.
ACES-GNN improves prediction accuracy for activity cliff molecules, reducing RMSE_cliff.
A positive correlation exists between the improvement in prediction accuracy and the improvement in explanation quality.
The ACES framework is effective across different GNN backbones (MPNN, GIN, GAT).
Explanation supervision helps the model focus on uncommon substructures critical for activity cliffs, aligning attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The ground-truth coloring relies on a fixed definition for activity cliff molecules, and some uncommon substructures between pairs may not be causative for potency changes.
The current GNN backbone does not outperform the Random Forest + ECFP combination in predictive accuracy or attribution quality across all datasets.
The validation process prioritizes minimizing RMSE during training rather than optimizing the explainability metric, so not all attributions after supervision achieve higher global direction accuracy.
future_direction: Incorporate geometric information into GNNs for further improvement.
Explore alternative gradient-based explanation techniques, such as expected gradients, to reduce potential biases.
Develop methods to identify true causal substructures in activity cliffs, enhancing explanation evaluation and guidance.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized molecular property prediction by leveraging graph-based representations, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder broader adoption in drug discovery. This study introduces the Activity-Cliff-Explanation-Supervised GNN (ACES-GNN) framework, designed to simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating explanation supervision for activity cliffs (ACs) into GNN training. ACs, defined by structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences, pose challenges for traditional models due to their reliance on shared structural features. By aligning model attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations, the ACES-GNN framework bridges the gap between prediction and explanation. Validated across 30 pharmacological targets, ACES-GNN consistently enhances both predictive accuracy and attribution quality for ACs compared to unsupervised GNNs. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between improved predictions and accurate explanations, offering a robust and adaptable framework to better understand and interpret ACs. This work underscores the potential of explanation-guided learning to advance interpretable artificial intelligence in molecular modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Models: Fast, Interpretable Generative Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we design latent priors for generative models that are efficient, stable, interpretable, and can incorporate domain knowledge, bridging the trade-off between simple priors and costly iterative samplers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Model (KAEM), a generative model that uses a univariate latent structure based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem to enable fast, exact inference via inverse transform sampling and offers interpretability of the learned prior.
papers.conclusion: KAEM is a promising step towards interpretable generative models that combine fast inference, competitive sample quality, and the potential for incorporating structural inductive biases, laying groundwork for further exploration of the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem in machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
KAEM enables fast and exact inference via inverse transform sampling, avoiding costly Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.
Importance sampling becomes a viable and efficient training strategy for simple datasets due to the low-dimensional latent space.
For complex datasets, a population-based sampling strategy using thermodynamic integration and power posteriors improves mixing and exploration.
KAEM generates samples of competitive quality compared to VAEs on SVHN and CelebA datasets.
The learned univariate priors are interpretable and can be visualized, offering a path for latent discovery and knowledge transfer.
papers.limitation:
Training with Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) does not scale efficiently on GPUs due to its iterative, gradient-based nature and irregular memory access patterns.
Importance sampling fails on complex datasets (e.g., SVHN, CelebA) due to prior-posterior mismatch, necessitating the use of ULA.
The search operations required for inverse transform sampling and residual resampling are difficult to parallelize on GPUs, leading to suboptimal performance.
future_direction: Utilizing the XPU, a reconfigurable dataflow accelerator, for more efficient implementation of KAEM's univariate structure and sampling operations.
Expanding the role of importance sampling by learning in a reduced-order space (e.g., via PCA) or incorporating domain knowledge to shape the prior.
Improving expressivity by exploring different KAN bases, mixture-of-experts frameworks, and domain-specific inductive biases.
papers.abstract: Generative models typically rely on either simple latent priors (e.g., Variational Autoencoders, VAEs), which are efficient but limited, or highly expressive iterative samplers (e.g., Diffusion and Energy-based Models), which are costly and opaque. We introduce the Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Model (KAEM) to bridge this trade-off and provide a new avenue for latent-space interpretability. Based on a novel interpretation of the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem, which provides new structural biases for generative modeling, KAEM imposes a univariate latent structure that enables fast and exact inference via the inverse transform method. With a low-dimensional latent space and appropriate inductive biases, we show that importance sampling becomes a viable, unbiased, and highly efficient posterior inference method. For settings where importance sampling fails, we propose a population-based strategy that decomposes the posterior into a sequence of annealed distributions to improve mixing during sampling, a common pitfall in Energy-based Models. We present initial comparisons of KAEM against VAEs for the SVHN and CelebA datasets, demonstrating its potential for competitive sample quality, inference speed, and interpretability.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically label neurons in protein language models with natural language descriptions, and how can these labels be used to steer protein generation towards desired properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated neuron labeling framework for protein language models and a neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired biochemical and structural properties.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for automated neuron labeling and generative steering in protein language models, enabling interpretability and control over protein generation, and suggests future directions for integration with structural validation and model pruning.
papers.key_findings:
Automated neuron labeling produces interpretable descriptions that capture diverse biochemical and structural properties of proteins.
Neuron activation-guided steering can generate proteins with targeted characteristics, such as specific molecular weight, GRAVY score, and secondary/tertiary structural motifs.
Larger PLMs capture more fine-grained protein features and show a more distributed representation of features across layers compared to smaller models.
Feature encoding follows a hierarchical pattern: sequence-derived properties peak in early layers, structural properties in middle layers, and functional properties in later layers.
Negative steering (multiplying neuron activations by negative values) can invert the effect for some features (e.g., GRAVY score) but not for others (e.g., instability index).
papers.limitation:
LLM explainer may generate oversimplified or hallucinated descriptions.
Generated proteins may not fold into viable, stable structures due to high ΔG values.
Limited to three models due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Incorporate a reinforcement learning module with structure prediction models (e.g., AlphaFold2) to improve structural viability of generated proteins.
Extend neuron labeling to more models and use multiple LLMs for more robust labels.
Explore pruning neurons based on labels to compress models while retaining performance.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) encode rich biological information, yet their internal neuron representations are poorly understood. We introduce the first automated framework for labeling every neuron in a PLM with biologically grounded natural language descriptions. Unlike prior approaches relying on sparse autoencoders or manual annotation, our method scales to hundreds of thousands of neurons, revealing individual neurons are selectively sensitive to diverse biochemical and structural properties. We then develop a novel neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired traits, enabling convergence to target biochemical properties like molecular weight and instability index as well as secondary and tertiary structural motifs, including alpha helices and canonical Zinc Fingers. We finally show that analysis of labeled neurons in different model sizes reveals PLM scaling laws and a structured neuron space distribution.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Grokking vs. Learning: Same Features, Different Encodings
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental differences between models learned via grokking and ordinary steady training? Are there any practical advantages to grokking?
papers.core_contribution: Grokked and steadily trained models learn the same features, but there can be large differences in the efficiency of encoding. A novel compressive regime in steady learning shows a linear trade-off between loss and compressibility.
papers.conclusion: Grokking and steady learning lead to models with the same features but different encodings, and grokking is not inherently more compressed. The dynamics of grokking are task-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Grokked and steadily learned models learn the same features (energy for Ising, Fourier for modular addition).
In modular addition, steady learning exhibits a compressive regime with a linear trade-off between train loss and compressibility, achieving compression factors up to 25x.
Model development during grokking is task-dependent: in modular addition, features develop during the plateau; in Ising, no development before generalization.
Grokking trajectories follow an approximately straight line in model space as defined by the Fisher Information Metric.
Peak compressibility is achieved immediately after the grokking plateau.
papers.abstract: Grokking typically achieves similar loss to ordinary, "steady", learning. We ask whether these different learning paths - grokking versus ordinary training - lead to fundamental differences in the learned models. To do so we compare the features, compressibility, and learning dynamics of models trained via each path in two tasks. We find that grokked and steadily trained models learn the same features, but there can be large differences in the efficiency with which these features are encoded. In particular, we find a novel "compressive regime" of steady training in which there emerges a linear trade-off between model loss and compressibility, and which is absent in grokking. In this regime, we can achieve compression factors 25x times the base model, and 5x times the compression achieved in grokking. We then track how model features and compressibility develop through training. We show that model development in grokking is task-dependent, and that peak compressibility is achieved immediately after the grokking plateau. Finally, novel information-geometric measures are introduced which demonstrate that models undergoing grokking follow a straight path in information space.

papers.title: Learning Invariances in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we automatically discover the appropriate symmetries (invariances and equivariances) in neural networks from training data alone?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Augerino, a method to learn invariances and equivariances in neural networks by learning a distribution over augmentations from training data alone.
papers.conclusion: Augerino is a framework that can learn symmetries from training data alone and improve generalization across various tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Augerino can learn the correct set and extent of invariances from training data alone, including full invariance (rotMNIST), soft invariance (Mario & Iggy), and no invariance (Olivetti faces).
Augerino improves test accuracy on CIFAR-10 compared to fixed augmentations and is competitive with Fast AutoAugment.
Augerino improves molecular property prediction on QM9, competitive with hand-chosen augmentations.
Augerino can learn equivariances for semantic segmentation on rotCamVid.
Augerino solutions are flatter in the loss landscape, which explains better generalization.
papers.abstract: Invariances to translations have imbued convolutional neural networks with powerful generalization properties. However, we often do not know a priori what invariances are present in the data, or to what extent a model should be invariant to a given symmetry group. We show how to \emph{learn} invariances and equivariances by parameterizing a distribution over augmentations and optimizing the training loss simultaneously with respect to the network parameters and augmentation parameters. With this simple procedure we can recover the correct set and extent of invariances on image classification, regression, segmentation, and molecular property prediction from a large space of augmentations, on training data alone.

papers.title: Learning Invariances for Interpretability using Supervised VAE
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a model by learning its invariant transformations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a supervised variational autoencoder (VAE) to simultaneously learn a classifier and a generative model for its invariances, enabling model interpretation by generating samples that leave the classification unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach to interpretability by learning a model's invariances via a supervised VAE, which can generate invariant samples and be integrated with feature attribution methods for more detailed explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Supervised VAE (SV AE) outperforms the Semi-Supervised V AE (SemiV AE) baseline in classification accuracy, especially on harder tasks.
The parameter β in the SV AE allows a trade-off between generative and discriminative performance, with higher β improving reconstruction at the potential cost of classification accuracy on difficult tasks.
The SV AE is more robust to changes in the invariant (nuisance) latent dimensions compared to the SemiV AE baseline.
By generating invariant samples and comparing them to the original via feature attribution methods (e.g., GradientShap), the method can highlight both unimportant and important features for a classification decision.
The method can efficiently generate counterfactual explanations by perturbing the classification-specific latent dimensions, avoiding the need for per-sample optimization.
future_direction: Applying the method to high-dimensional data without clear semantic, such as long genomic sequences.
Exploring explicit parametrization of invariances, potentially using Bayesian methods to learn the distribution over transformation parameters.
papers.abstract: We propose to learn model invariances as a means of interpreting a model. This is motivated by a reverse engineering principle. If we understand a problem, we may introduce inductive biases in our model in the form of invariances. Conversely, when interpreting a complex supervised model, we can study its invariances to understand how that model solves a problem. To this end we propose a supervised form of variational auto-encoders (VAEs). Crucially, only a subset of the dimensions in the latent space contributes to the supervised task, allowing the remaining dimensions to act as nuisance parameters. By sampling solely the nuisance dimensions, we are able to generate samples that have undergone transformations that leave the classification unchanged, revealing the invariances of the model. Our experimental results show the capability of our proposed model both in terms of classification, and generation of invariantly transformed samples. Finally we show how combining our model with feature attribution methods it is possible to reach a more fine-grained understanding about the decision process of the model.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Multimodal Representation Collapse
papers.research_question: Why do models trained for multimodal fusion tend to rely only on a subset of modalities, ignoring the rest (modality collapse), and how can this be prevented?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical understanding of modality collapse as arising from cross-modal polysemantic interference due to rank bottlenecks, and proposes Explicit Basis Reallocation (EBR) to prevent collapse by disentangling and denoising multimodal representations.
papers.conclusion: Modality collapse in multimodal fusion can be understood and effectively prevented through basis reallocation, which disentangles cross-modal feature entanglements and denoises representations, leading to robust multimodal learning.
papers.key_findings:
Modality collapse is caused by cross-modal polysemantic interference where noisy features from one modality entangle with predictive features from another via shared neurons in the fusion head.
This interference is a consequence of low-rank simplicity bias in neural networks, which creates rank bottlenecks in gradient updates.
Cross-modal knowledge distillation implicitly mitigates collapse by freeing up rank bottlenecks, allowing independent denoising of modalities.
Explicit Basis Reallocation (EBR) explicitly disentangles and denoises modalities by reallocating basis vectors, preventing collapse and enabling robust handling of missing modalities.
EBR achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks with missing modalities.
papers.limitation: Theoretical results rely on the identifiability condition of modality-specific causal factors.
papers.abstract: We aim to develop a fundamental understanding of modality collapse, a recently observed empirical phenomenon wherein models trained for multimodal fusion tend to rely only on a subset of the modalities, ignoring the rest. We show that modality collapse happens when noisy features from one modality are entangled, via a shared set of neurons in the fusion head, with predictive features from another, effectively masking out positive contributions from the predictive features of the former modality and leading to its collapse. We further prove that cross-modal knowledge distillation implicitly disentangles such representations by freeing up rank bottlenecks in the student encoder, denoising the fusion-head outputs without negatively impacting the predictive features from either modality. Based on the above findings, we propose an algorithm that prevents modality collapse through explicit basis reallocation, with applications in dealing with missing modalities. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal benchmarks validate our theoretical claims. Project page: https://abhrac.github.io/mmcollapse/.

papers.title: Investigating Navigation Strategies in the Morris Water Maze through Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How do deep reinforcement learning agents learn navigation in a simulated Morris Water Maze, and how do their strategies and internal representations compare to biological agents?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a 2D simulation of the Morris Water Maze for deep RL, shows that agents develop navigation strategies similar to biological agents, and that auxiliary tasks can improve learning and lead to the development of internal representations resembling place and head-direction cells.
papers.conclusion: The 2D simulated Morris Water Maze is an effective environment for studying navigation in deep RL, and auxiliary tasks can improve learning and lead to the development of biologically plausible internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Agents trained in different MWM variations develop different strategy preferences, and the learning dynamics (from non-spatial to spatial strategies) resemble those in rodents and humans.
Auxiliary tasks, especially categorical ones, improve the final policy performance by encouraging spatial strategies and reducing reliance on circling.
The Explore Bonus auxiliary task improves early learning rates.
Agents develop internal representations (in neural activations) sensitive to spatial location and direction, similar to place cells and head-direction cells.
The presence of direction-sensitive representations correlates with increased direct navigation strategy usage and performance.
papers.limitation:
The representation scores have limitations: they are not designed to be sensitive to activation patterns that are periodic in space or direction.
Correlations between representation scores and performance may also be task dependent.
The behavior classifier is not perfectly accurate, with some trajectories falling into multiple categories.
future_direction: Investigating why auxiliary tasks improve performance by quantifying task difficulty and learning exposure.
Exploring the use of pre-trained networks with frozen representations for new agents.
Testing predictions about human navigation in square mazes and with auxiliary tasks.
papers.abstract: Navigation is a complex skill with a long history of research in animals and humans. In this work, we simulate the Morris Water Maze in 2D to train deep reinforcement learning agents. We perform automatic classification of navigation strategies, analyze the distribution of strategies used by artificial agents, and compare them with experimental data to show similar learning dynamics as those seen in humans and rodents. We develop environment-specific auxiliary tasks and examine factors affecting their usefulness. We suggest that the most beneficial tasks are potentially more biologically feasible for real agents to use. Lastly, we explore the development of internal representations in the activations of artificial agent neural networks. These representations resemble place cells and head-direction cells found in mouse brains, and their presence has correlation to the navigation strategies that artificial agents employ.

papers.title: Identification of state functions by physically-guided neural networks with physically-meaningful internal layers
papers.research_question: How to predict the input-output relation in a physical system while fulfilling physical constraints, and how to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Physically-Guided Neural Networks with Internal Variables (PGNNIV), a method that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to predict system behavior and infer internal state variables, showing improved convergence, data efficiency, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: PGNNIV is a promising framework that combines the predictive power of neural networks with physical interpretability, and shows advantages over standard neural networks in terms of convergence, data needs, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.key_findings:
The method accelerates the training process.
It reduces the amount of data required for similar accuracy.
It filters noise in experimental data.
It provides improved extrapolation capacity.
It allows obtaining internal state variables without additional assumptions.
papers.limitation:
For deep neural models, large and varied data are needed.
Defining successful network topology and hyperparameters is complex and time-consuming.
Predictions may not be as accurate as using full prescribed mathematical models.
papers.abstract: Substitution of well-grounded theoretical models by data-driven predictions is not as simple in engineering and sciences as it is in social and economic fields. Scientific problems suffer most times from paucity of data, while they may involve a large number of variables and parameters that interact in complex and non-stationary ways, obeying certain physical laws. Moreover, a physically-based model is not only useful for making predictions, but to gain knowledge by the interpretation of its structure, parameters, and mathematical properties. The solution to these shortcomings seems to be the seamless blending of the tremendous predictive power of the data-driven approach with the scientific consistency and interpretability of physically-based models. We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: Controlling generative models with continuous factors of variations
papers.research_question: How to find interpretable directions in the latent space of generative models to control continuous factors of variations such as position and scale of objects in generated images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to find interpretable directions in the latent space of generative models that correspond to continuous factors of variations, enabling precise control over properties like object position and scale without human annotations.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method to extract meaningful directions in the latent space of generative models, enabling precise control over factors like translation and scale, which advances interpretability of latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can control horizontal and vertical position and scale of objects in generated images from BigGAN and β-VAE.
The directions for factors like position and scale are shared across different object categories in BigGAN.
In BigGAN, spatial factors of variation are mainly encoded in the first part of the hierarchical latent code.
Disentangled representations (achieved with higher β in β-VAE) lead to more precise control over factors.
The proposed reconstruction loss with frequency weighting produces sharper reconstructions and improves inversion of generative models.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on simple transformations like position and scale; more sophisticated transformations are not tested.
For large scales, the algorithm fails due to poor performance of the saliency model when the object covers almost the entire image.
future_direction: Adapt the method to other factors of variations such as rotations, brightness, contrast, color, or local deformations.
Use the method to analyze distributions of factors in training datasets to reveal potential bias.
papers.abstract: Recent deep generative models are able to provide photo-realistic images as well as visual or textual content embeddings useful to address various tasks of computer vision and natural language processing. Their usefulness is nevertheless often limited by the lack of control over the generative process or the poor understanding of the learned representation. To overcome these major issues, very recent work has shown the interest of studying the semantics of the latent space of generative models. In this paper, we propose to advance on the interpretability of the latent space of generative models by introducing a new method to find meaningful directions in the latent space of any generative model along which we can move to control precisely specific properties of the generated image like the position or scale of the object in the image. Our method does not require human annotations and is particularly well suited for the search of directions encoding simple transformations of the generated image, such as translation, zoom or color variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method qualitatively and quantitatively, both for GANs and variational auto-encoders.

papers.title: Inducing Sparse Coding and And-Or Grammar from Generator Network
papers.research_question: How can we fuse the sparse coding model and the generator network to obtain an explainable generative model with meaningful hierarchical representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a sparse generative model that combines the generator network and sparse coding, inducing an AND-OR grammar and learning meaningful, explainable hierarchical representations from images.
papers.conclusion: The proposed model naturally combines the generator network and sparse coding model while maintaining their advantages, learning meaningful hierarchical representations.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns meaningful dictionaries at different layers, with bottom-layer kernels capturing primitives like edges and object parts, and top-layer kernels combining these into whole objects.
The sparse activations in the feature maps can be interpreted as coefficients in a sparse coding framework, and the generating process can be described as an AND-OR parsing graph.
The model maintains the advantages of both the generator network (efficient learning and realistic generation) and sparse coding (meaningful basis functions).
papers.abstract: We introduce an explainable generative model by applying sparse operation on the feature maps of the generator network. Meaningful hierarchical representations are obtained using the proposed generative model with sparse activations. The convolutional kernels from the bottom layer to the top layer of the generator network can learn primitives such as edges and colors, object parts, and whole objects layer by layer. From the perspective of the generator network, we propose a method for inducing both sparse coding and the AND-OR grammar for images. Experiments show that our method is capable of learning meaningful and explainable hierarchical representations.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: A Multi-Agent Framework Integrating Large Language Models and Generative AI for Accelerated Metamaterial Design
papers.research_question: How can a multi-agent framework integrating large language models and generative AI accelerate and improve the design of metamaterials?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CrossMatAgent, a multi-agent framework that integrates LLMs and generative AI to automate metamaterial design, enabling high-fidelity, simulation-ready pattern generation.
papers.conclusion: CrossMatAgent establishes a scalable, AI-driven paradigm for accelerated metamaterial development, automating design generation and enhancing fidelity for practical applications.
papers.key_findings:
The multi-agent system can generate diverse and manufacturable metamaterial designs from various input formats.
Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL on the augmented dataset produces high-quality, reproducible designs suitable for computational simulation and 3D printing.
SHAP analysis demonstrates that the fine-tuned CLIP model has enhanced understanding of geometrical patterns compared to the base model.
CrossMatAgent outperforms traditional generative methods like DALL-E 3 and base SDXL in generating clear, stable, and reproducible metamaterial patterns.
The framework bridges the gap between conceptual design and practical realization, reducing reliance on trial-and-error methods.
papers.limitation: The dataset size is constrained by the iterative nature of prompt engineering, requiring multiple generation cycles and increasing API-related computational costs.
papers.abstract: Metamaterials, renowned for their exceptional mechanical, electromagnetic, and thermal properties, hold transformative potential across diverse applications, yet their design remains constrained by labor-intensive trial-and-error methods and limited data interoperability. Here, we introduce CrossMatAgent -- a novel multi-agent framework that synergistically integrates large language models with state-of-the-art generative AI to revolutionize metamaterial design. By orchestrating a hierarchical team of agents -- each specializing in tasks such as pattern analysis, architectural synthesis, prompt engineering, and supervisory feedback -- our system leverages the multimodal reasoning of GPT-4o alongside the generative precision of DALL-E 3 and a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion XL model. This integrated approach automates data augmentation, enhances design fidelity, and produces simulation- and 3D printing-ready metamaterial patterns. Comprehensive evaluations, including CLIP-based alignment, SHAP interpretability analyses, and mechanical simulations under varied load conditions, demonstrate the framework's ability to generate diverse, reproducible, and application-ready designs. CrossMatAgent thus establishes a scalable, AI-driven paradigm that bridges the gap between conceptual innovation and practical realization, paving the way for accelerated metamaterial development.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Part-Based Representation of Data Using Sparse Autoencoders With Nonnegativity Constraints
papers.research_question: How can nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training be used to learn part-based representations of data, and does this improve reconstruction and prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (NCAE) for training autoencoders that learns part-based, sparse features, improving reconstruction quality and the prediction performance of deep networks.
papers.conclusion: Nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training enable part-based representation learning, which improves reconstruction and classification performance in deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Nonnegativity constraints force autoencoders to learn features that capture a part-based representation of data.
NCAE achieves lower reconstruction error and better sparsity in hidden encoding compared to SAE and NMF.
A deep network pre-trained with NCAE achieves better classification accuracy than networks pre-trained with SAE, NNSAE, DAE, and DpAE on several datasets.
The learned features (receptive fields) are more interpretable, representing parts like strokes in digits or facial features.
The method works for both image and text data, extracting semantic features from documents.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a new deep learning autoencoder network, trained by a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (nonnegativity-constrained autoencoder), that learns features that show part-based representation of data. The learning algorithm is based on constraining negative weights. The performance of the algorithm is assessed based on decomposing data into parts and its prediction performance is tested on three standard image data sets and one text data set. The results indicate that the nonnegativity constraint forces the autoencoder to learn features that amount to a part-based representation of data, while improving sparsity and reconstruction quality in comparison with the traditional sparse autoencoder and nonnegative matrix factorization. It is also shown that this newly acquired representation improves the prediction performance of a deep neural network.

papers.title: Generative Model Inversion Through the Lens of the Manifold Hypothesis
papers.research_question: What is the reason behind the effectiveness of generative model inversion attacks? The paper hypothesizes that models are more vulnerable when loss gradients align with the generator manifold.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric analysis of generative model inversion, showing it acts as gradient denoising via projection onto the generator manifold, and introduces AlignMI, a training-free method to enhance gradient-manifold alignment, improving inversion attacks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gradient-manifold alignment is a key factor in model inversion vulnerability and that the proposed AlignMI method effectively enhances inversion attacks by improving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Generative model inversion implicitly denoises gradients by projecting them onto the generator manifold.
Models are more vulnerable to MIAs when loss gradients align more closely with the generator manifold.
The proposed AlignMI method (with PAA and TAA) improves inversion performance over state-of-the-art generative MIAs.
Alignment-aware training increases model vulnerability to MIAs, validating the hypothesis.
There is a trade-off between gradient-manifold alignment and predictive performance.
papers.limitation:
Alignment-aware training is currently feasible only in low-resolution settings due to computational constraints.
There is a trade-off between alignment and predictive performance, and the cause of this trade-off is unclear.
future_direction: Investigating the alignment-accuracy trade-off.
Developing defenses by reducing gradient-manifold alignment.
papers.abstract: Model inversion attacks (MIAs) aim to reconstruct class-representative samples from trained models. Recent generative MIAs utilize generative adversarial networks to learn image priors that guide the inversion process, yielding reconstructions with high visual quality and strong fidelity to the private training data. To explore the reason behind their effectiveness, we begin by examining the gradients of inversion loss with respect to synthetic inputs, and find that these gradients are surprisingly noisy. Further analysis reveals that generative inversion implicitly denoises these gradients by projecting them onto the tangent space of the generator manifold, filtering out off-manifold components while preserving informative directions aligned with the manifold. Our empirical measurements show that, in models trained with standard supervision, loss gradients often exhibit large angular deviations from the data manifold, indicating poor alignment with class-relevant directions. This observation motivates our central hypothesis: models become more vulnerable to MIAs when their loss gradients align more closely with the generator manifold. We validate this hypothesis by designing a novel training objective that explicitly promotes such alignment. Building on this insight, we further introduce a training-free approach to enhance gradient-manifold alignment during inversion, leading to consistent improvements over state-of-the-art generative MIAs.

papers.title: Integrating geometries of ReLU feedforward neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to analyze the geometric properties (polyhedral decomposition) of ReLU feedforward neural networks and uses this to study network behavior, including adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a toolbox for analyzing the polyhedral decomposition of ReLU feedforward neural networks and uses it to study geometric properties, including Hamming distance, bisection method, and Chebyshev centers, providing insights into network behavior and adversarial examples.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a toolbox and methodologies for analyzing the geometries of ReLU neural networks, offering insights into their structure, behavior, and response to adversarial inputs, and serves as a foundation for future analysis on larger datasets and more complex architectures.
papers.key_findings:
